article.title: Failed Housing System
article.author: Dick Platkin
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Los Angeles has a new mayor, Nithya Raman, who will soon be sworn into her four year mayoral term. Can we assume things will then improve, especially regarding the homeless and overcrowded? In a word, NO. This is why. Nithya Raman presented a reduction in the number of homeless people as a success in her fourth Council District, but this statistic has two problems. First, the process which creates widespread and increasing homeless not only remains, but is increasing. Second, her actions did not include the overcrowded, who number over a million in the Los Angeles region. Together, the increasing homeless and overcrowded numbers reveal the inherent problems her and other elected officials face in making sure all Angelenos have an adequate place to live. The reason is not a shortage of vacant apartments or even houses. For example in my older Los Angeles neighborhood, near Wilshire Boulevard and the new D subway line , there is a vacant apartment on nearly every block. The homeless and overcrowded would gladly move into these vacant apartments if they could afford them. But they cannot come up with the first month’s rent, damage deposit, and last month’s rent. If they had enough savings, they would be able to rent a vacant apartment, but they can’t afford to. The barrier is not supply, but the dire financial situation of the homeless and overcrowded. Is there a solution this problem? Of course there is, but it is no longer available. The answer is public housing, a signature feature of the New Deal. These programs began in the mid-1930’s and ended in the early 1970’s, when the Nixon administration (1968 – 1973), with the eventual support of Congressional Democrats, ended these HUD housing programs. Nevertheless, some public housing survives in the United States as older housing that has not yet been shut down to make way for private sector housing. In Los Angeles, for example, there still is available public housing, but it is around 50 or more years old. What is now available had to be built before 1970. Related: Over-crowded Homes in LA County and How to Help Them In some cities, like Seattle, most public housing projects, such as Holly Park, have been demolished and replaced with private sector housing. In Los Angeles, a few public housing projects survive, but they are still hanging on until they too give way to private sector housing. The solution: A few European countries, like Austria and Finland, still have publicly built and operated housing, so we know that it is still possible. But public housing is not in the cards for the USA. Even Bernie Sanders, the 85 year old Independent Senator from Vermont, no longer proposes HUD (Dept. of Urban Affairs) public housing on his website . Related: Living in Cars: LA's Hidden Homelessness Crisis Unfortunately without the resurrection of public housing in this country, we will witness increasing levels of homelessness and overcrowding, like the current situation in Los Angeles. Knowing that public housing programs offer a viable alternative give us something to propose to the new Democratic majorities in the Senate and the House. My advice to you is not to hold your breath because, however, the Democratic politicians in DC, like the new Mayor in LA, are not about to call for a return of HUD public housing programs.
